prompt: A forum saves each post's body to the database and inserts it directly into the HTML the server generates, without encoding. A user's post contains script that runs for every reader. What type of XSS is this?

options.explanation: Reflected XSS echoes input from the *current request*. Here the payload was saved and served later to other users.
Client-side sink insertion would make it DOM-based too, but this question specifies that the server inserts it. Stored versus reflected is a separate way of sorting XSS.
Correct. The payload is persisted on the server and delivered to every viewer, with no crafted link needed.

options.text: Not XSS, because the attacker didn't send anything to the victim
options.explanation: XSS needs only that attacker-controlled data executes in the victim's browser in your origin. Stored XSS needs no direct contact with the victim.

workedExample: The payload persists in the database and is delivered on later views, so it is stored XSS. Here the server inserts it into HTML. Persisted data inserted unsafely by client JavaScript could instead be both stored and DOM-based; URL data can also feed a DOM sink.

prompt:
This search handler pastes the query into HTML: ```python q = request.args.get("q", "") return f"

Results for {q}

" ``` Four fixes are proposed. Which one is the correct fix for this bug?

options.text: Strip `<script>` tags from `q` with a regular expression
options.explanation: Filtering out known-bad patterns misses other ways to run script, such as an image with an `onerror` attribute, and regex HTML filtering is easy to bypass. It also silently changes legitimate text.

options.text: Pass `q` as a parameter instead, as you would in a parameterised SQL query
options.explanation: Parameterised queries are the right fix for SQL injection, because the database receives code and data separately. Here `q` never reaches SQL, and a server-built HTML page has no placeholder: the browser parses the whole response as one document.

options.text: HTML-encode `q` where it is output, with `escape(q)` or an auto-escaping template, so `<` becomes `<`
options.explanation: Correct. Encoding for the HTML text context makes the browser display special characters instead of parsing them as markup. An auto-escaping template does this by default.

That is the encoding for URL components, not HTML text. It would show users `%3C` and `%20` instead of their search, and choosing the encoding by habit rather than by context is exactly the mistake that causes XSS elsewhere.

workedExample: 1. Name the destination: `q` lands in **HTML text**, between tags. 2. Pick the defence for that context: HTML output encoding. 3. Check the effect, for example `escape("Tom & Jerry")`: ``` <b>Tom & Jerry</b> ``` The browser shows the characters `Tom & Jerry` as plain visible text, not bold text, so data stays data. 4. Compare with SQL: there, the strongest fix is a parameterised query, and OWASP discourages manual escaping. HTML pages have no such channel, so encoding (ideally automatic, in the template) is the standard defence.

options.text: Yes, because all output is now escaped
options.explanation: The vulnerable output is produced by client JS, not the server. Server-side escaping never touches this value.

options.text: No: ordinary HTTP navigation omits the fragment, and this value reaches innerHTML in client code; use a text sink or suitable sanitisation
options.explanation: Correct for this data flow. Escaping values in the server's HTML never transforms the fragment before this sink. Replace innerHTML with textContent for ordinary text; server-supplied CSP can provide additional defence.

options.text: Yes, if they also add a WAF rule blocking `<script>` in URLs
options.explanation: A WAF never sees the fragment either, and `innerHTML` payloads don't need a `<script>` tag (event-handler attributes work).
`decodeURIComponent` only decodes percent-escapes into a string. The sink, `innerHTML`, is the problem.

workedExample:
Trace the data flow:

```
URL  /page#<payload>
      |  fragment stays in browser
      v
location.hash (source)
      |
      v
box.innerHTML (sink) -> parsed as HTML
```

No value from the server's HTML is on this source-to-sink path, so output escaping on the server misses it. Replace the sink:

```javascript
// Replace content without HTML parsing.
box.textContent = t;
```

Or, if HTML is genuinely needed, `box.innerHTML = DOMPurify.sanitize(t)`.
